findings.issue_text: [BUG] The added line `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` references `organization_context`, which is not a parameter of `get()`, not imported in this module, and not assigned anywhere in the method, so every non-superuser GET raises NameError. The audit-log endpoint returns a 500 for every request by a non-superuser, because the assignment executes unconditionally even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested; superusers short-circuit past the right operand and instead hit the OptimizedCursorPaginator construction failure at paginate time.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator, whose __init__ has no `order_by` parameter and requires an explicit `key`, so the endpoint's `self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by="-datetime", ...)` raises TypeError('__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument order_by') as soon as the optimized path is taken. Superuser requests with optimized_pagination=true crash with a 500; the class can never be constructed through the standard paginate() path, which forwards order_by into the paginator constructor (the existing DateTimePaginator call in this same endpoint depends on exactly that forwarding).

[BUG] get_result calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)`, but BasePaginator does not implement build_queryset (only the Paginator subclass does), so the call raises NotImplementedError on first invocation. Even if the constructor incompatibility is fixed, every request routed to OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes before returning any results; the class has no working query-building path.

[BUG] get_result calls `build_cursor(...)`, a function that is neither defined in sentry/api/paginator.py nor imported anywhere in this diff (every existing paginator in this file constructs CursorResult directly, as the unchanged tail at line 817 shows), so get_result raises NameError. Even after fixing construction and build_queryset, the class crashes with NameError on every call; the advertised 'enhanced cursor handling' cannot execute.

[BUG] The 'advanced' negative-offset branch executes `list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative start_offset, which Django QuerySets do not support — QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') — so the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any cursor with a negative offset (client-craftable via the cursor query parameter) reaching this branch crashes the request with a 500; the advertised negative-offset pagination feature cannot work against a Django queryset at all.

[BUG] The script switches span-buf:s:* keys from SET to ZSET semantics (scard/sunionstore replaced by zcard/zunionstore) with no migration or version guard, so during a rolling deploy zcard/zunionstore run against keys still written as SETs by pre-deploy workers and Redis aborts the script with WRONGTYPE. Span-buffer writes fail for every trace whose keys were created by old workers (the whole Lua script aborts, dropping the batch's redirect resolution and merge work) until legacy keys age out via the set_timeout TTL.

[BUG] process_spans now issues ZADD (and _load_segment_data issues ZSCAN at line 434) against span-buf:s:* keys that pre-deploy Lua/Python writers created as SETs, so redis-py raises a WRONGTYPE ResponseError during the deploy window. Span ingestion and flush errors for any key not yet migrated — the consumer-side half of the same make-before-break gap as the Lua script, hitting old-worker-created keys in both the write and flush-read paths.

[BUG] process_batch reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` unconditionally, but the field is optional in the ingest_spans_v1 span schema, so any span event produced without it raises KeyError. After deploy, the process consumer crashes on messages already retained in the topic (and on events from producers not yet emitting the field), failing the batch and dropping or stalling span processing depending on the consumer's error handling.

[ADVISORY] The new clamp only covers non-prev cursors (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`), so a prev cursor with a negative offset still slices the queryset negatively and raises AssertionError, while a crafted non-prev negative cursor now silently returns page 1 — neither behavior matches the added comment claiming the queryset 'will handle boundary conditions'. Operators debugging 500s from malformed cursors get false guidance from the comment, and malformed-cursor behavior is inconsistently split between prev (500) and non-prev (silent first page).

[ADVISORY] The diff adds OptimizedCursorPaginator and the endpoint's optimized_pagination branch with no test anywhere in the diff (all added tests are spans-buffer tests), so none of the construction, build_queryset, build_cursor, or negative-slicing failures are exercised by CI. The broken paginator ships green, and future fixes to it land equally untested; a regression in the optimized path would again only surface as production 500s.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator re-declares get_item_key and value_from_cursor verbatim from BasePaginator and copies BasePaginator.get_result wholesale except for one branch; subclassing Paginator — which already supplies order_by handling, key derivation, build_queryset, and count_hits — would delete roughly 60 duplicated lines and remove the order_by/build_queryset incompatibilities. Every future change to the base get_result logic must be manually mirrored in this copy or the two silently drift, which is exactly how the missing build_queryset slipped through here.

[ADVISORY] The new eviction path (zpopmin when span_count > 1000) has no test in the diff — no added test populates more than 1000 members — so the eviction arithmetic is unverified. A regression in the eviction count or score ordering would silently drop spans from buffered segments (permanent data loss for those spans) with no CI signal and no metric on the eviction path.

[ADVISORY] The audit-log pagination feature and the new paginator class are unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer insertion with eviction) yet are bundled into the same diff, so the spans optimization cannot ship, bisect, or revert independently of the broken pagination code. A revert of the pagination experiment also reverts the spans performance work and vice versa; the two changes' rollouts and failure domains are needlessly coupled.

[BUG] The new `enable_advanced` assignment references `organization_context`, a name that is neither imported nor defined anywhere in this diff, and the assignment executes unconditionally on every GET (only the `request.user.is_superuser` operand short-circuits past it). For every audit-log request from a non-superuser, evaluating `organization_context.member` raises NameError and the endpoint returns 500 instead of the listing — the existing endpoint breaks for all regular members, not just the new optimized path.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator and its get_result calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)`, but the class never defines build_queryset and BasePaginator provides no implementation (build_queryset exists only on CursorPaginator/DateTimePaginator). Every request with optimized_pagination=true raises AttributeError before any query runs, so the new paginator 500s on its only call site.

[BUG] The 'advanced feature' branch slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset, which Django rejects with `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the adjacent comment claiming the ORM 'handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any admin who sends a cursor with a negative offset gets a 500; the headline negative-offset pagination feature of this class can never return data.

[BUG] get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to `getattr(item, self.key)`, but the only call site paginates by the datetime column (`order_by='-datetime'`), so the key values are datetime objects, which math.floor rejects with TypeError — CursorPaginator's integer-key logic was copied onto a DateTimePaginator-style call site. Even once build_queryset is fixed, build_cursor raises TypeError computing the cursor key from the first result, so every optimized page 500s.

[BUG] The ~95-line OptimizedCursorPaginator and the new `optimized_pagination` endpoint branch ship with zero test coverage — the only test files touched in this diff are tests/sentry/spans/**, none of which import paginator or the audit-log endpoint. The defects above (missing build_queryset, datetime get_item_key, negative-offset AssertionError) all ship unverified; any future regression in the optimized path reaches production silently.

[BUG] The buffer migrates span sets from Redis SETs to ZSETs (zcard/zunionstore here, zadd in buffer.py:197, zscan in buffer.py:434) with no compatibility handling for keys written by the previous sadd/sunionstore code, which remain SET-typed until their TTL expires. During and after a rolling deploy, any trace whose buffered keys were written by old workers makes Redis return WRONGTYPE to zcard/zunionstore/zadd/zscan, failing span processing and flush batches until the stale keys expire under set_timeout.

[ADVISORY] Eviction permanently deletes the oldest buffered spans via zpopmin with no metric, log, or return value, and the same diff deletes the only count-overflow observability (the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric plus error log) from _load_segment_data. Span data loss becomes silent: operators investigating missing spans have no signal that eviction fired, whereas the pre-diff code logged and counted every skip.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises the eviction branch: the largest fixture in test_buffer.py inserts 5 spans, so the `span_count > 1000` zpopmin path and its interaction with the zunionstore merges are never executed. A regression in the eviction arithmetic (wrong count popped, or wrong end of the zset) would silently drop or retain wrong spans with CI green.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-resolution loop cap is cut from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the mis-resolution failure mode at the cap is deleted, so chains deeper than 1000 now stop resolving 10x earlier. Spans in very deep segment trees are filed under an intermediate ancestor's set instead of the segment root; no test in the diff covers chains beyond a few levels.

[ADVISORY] New pagination behavior is gated on a raw `optimized_pagination` query param with no options/feature-flag kill switch, and unauthorized users sending it silently get the old paginator. If the optimized path misbehaves in production it cannot be disabled without a code deploy, and clients receive different pagination semantics depending on role with no indication of the switch.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates CursorPaginator.get_result/get_item_key/value_from_cursor wholesale instead of subclassing CursorPaginator, and the copy has already drifted: wrong base class (losing build_queryset) and CursorPaginator's integer-only get_item_key carried to a datetime-keyed call site. Future fixes to CursorPaginator.get_result boundary handling will not propagate to the copy; subclassing and overriding only the offset branch would delete ~70 duplicated lines and eliminate two of the crashes.

[ADVISORY] Eviction exists only inside add-buffer.lua; the process_spans zadd path inserts spans into set keys with no eviction, and the same diff removes the flusher's count-based backstop (the max_segment_spans check in _load_segment_data), leaving the 1000-member cap unenforced on the Python insertion path. Sets grown past 1000 members via the zadd path are caught only by the byte-size guard, which skips and discards the entire segment's spans rather than evicting the oldest.

[ADVISORY] The change to the shared CursorPaginator.get_result claims the queryset 'will handle boundary conditions' for negative offsets, but the is_prev branch still passes negative offsets into the slice (AssertionError 500) while the non-prev branch silently clamps malformed cursors to page 1 — and no caller in this diff needs the change. All cursor-paginated endpoints inherit a half-implemented negative-offset policy under a comment that misstates Django's behavior, inviting future code to rely on 'negative offsets are safe'.

[ADVISORY] The required `end_timestamp_precise` field is inserted before the defaulted `is_segment_span` field in the Span NamedTuple, so any positional construction of Span with six arguments silently binds is_segment_span's value into end_timestamp_precise and leaves is_segment_span False. Call sites outside this diff that construct Span positionally produce spans silently misclassified as non-segment spans (wrong flush routing) instead of failing loudly with a missing-argument error.

[BUG] The audit-log endpoint's new 'optimized_pagination' feature (raw query-param gate, admin permission check, swap to a new OptimizedCursorPaginator) is unrelated work with no traceability to the PR's stated intent of optimizing spans buffer insertion with eviction. An unflagged, untested API behavior change ships to a shared endpoint inside a spans performance PR: spans reviewers will not scrutinize pagination code and vice versa, the feature cannot be independently rolled out or reverted (gated on a raw query param with no feature flag or options entry, so disabling it requires a code deploy), and the new paginator class plus the cursors.py comment changes ride along in shared infrastructure.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start index, which Django QuerySet rejects with AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') — the adjacent comment's claim that the ORM 'properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. An authorized admin using the optimized path with a negative-offset cursor (e.g. cursor=100:-5:0) gets a 500 instead of a page; the advertised advanced reverse-pagination feature cannot work at all.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator copies CursorPaginator's integer-key get_item_key/value_from_cursor instead of DateTimePaginator's datetime-to-epoch cursor conversion, so with the audit-log endpoint's 'datetime' key it calls math.floor/math.ceil directly on a datetime object. The first optimized_pagination=true request raises TypeError inside build_cursor (and cursor-value filtering compares a raw epoch integer against a DateTimeField), so the paginator swapped in for DateTimePaginator fails on real requests — it was never exercised against the contract of the class it replaces.

[BUG] The new enable_advanced line dereferences organization_context.member.has_global_access unconditionally on every GET, and organization_context.member is None for a superuser accessing an organization they are not a member of. Audit-log listing requests raise AttributeError and return a 500 for superusers without org membership — including plain requests that never set optimized_pagination — because the opt-in feature's permission check executes on the default code path (if organization_context is not imported in this module at all, the failure is a NameError on every request).

[BUG] The buffer's Redis keys (span-buf:s:*) change type from set to zset in place with no migration or version guard, so zcard/zunionstore/zscan now run against keys still stored as sets. At deploy time, pre-existing buffered spans written by the old code as sets, and old processor/flusher instances during a rolling deploy (old sadd/sscan against new zadd/zscan on the same key names), trigger Redis WRONGTYPE errors — span processing and flushing fail until the stale keys expire, delaying or dropping buffered spans.

[ADVISORY] BasePaginator.get_result's slicing is changed to clamp negative offsets to 0 for non-prev cursors — a silent behavior change to shared pagination infrastructure that is untraceable to the spans intent and only half-applied, since is_prev cursors with negative offsets still hit Django's negative-slice AssertionError. Every endpoint using a BasePaginator-derived paginator silently changes its failure mode for crafted negative-offset cursors from a 500 to a first-page response, with no test or documentation; the inconsistent half-fix leaves prev cursors crashing on the same input.

[ADVISORY] The parent-redirect resolution loop bound is tightened from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the resulting mis-join limitation is deleted. Traces with parent chains deeper than 1000 now stop resolving early and attach spans to an intermediate parent's set instead of the segment root — a 10x tightening of a previously documented correctness bound with no metric or note; operators debugging broken deep traces get no signal.

[ADVISORY] The max_segment_spans overflow guard (the skip-too-large-segment branch with its metric and logger.error) is deleted, leaving the max_segment_spans setting with no reader in this path while the effective count bound becomes the hardcoded 1000-per-set constant in add-buffer.lua. Operators tuning max_segment_spans get silently no effect; a segment composed of many parent sets (each up to 1000 spans) can exceed the old per-segment count limit and now flushes unbounded instead of being skipped with the segment_span_count_exceeded metric — two hand-maintained limits in Lua and Python settings with no shared source of truth.

[ADVISORY] The ~95-line OptimizedCursorPaginator class and the audit-log endpoint's new branching ship with zero test coverage in this diff, while every spans-side change in the same PR is test-updated. Any regression in the new paginator's cursor math, boundary handling, or advanced-features branch, or in the endpoint's permission gate, lands unobserved; the coverage asymmetry is itself evidence the pagination work was not developed against this repository's conventions.

[BUG] The endpoint evaluates `organization_context.member.has_global_access` on every GET (`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`), but no name `organization_context` is imported or defined anywhere in the module — the isort-ordered import block between `sentry.api.bases.organization` and `sentry.api.paginator` (exactly where a `sentry.api.helpers.*` import would sort) contains only the paginator import. Every non-superuser request to the audit-logs endpoint raises NameError before any pagination logic runs and returns 500 — the entire endpoint is broken for normal users; only superusers short-circuit the `or` and ever get a response.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` directly to `getattr(item, self.key)`, but its only call site passes `order_by='-datetime'` with no `key` override, so `self.key` resolves to the datetime model attribute (the same resolution DateTimePaginator relies on, whose get_item_key converts datetimes to ints before arithmetic) and `math.ceil(datetime)` raises TypeError. The first build_cursor call of every optimized-pagination request raises TypeError and the request 500s — the new paginator path cannot produce a single successful response, and no test in the diff exercises it.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), but Django QuerySet raises ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.') for any negative slice bound — the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any superuser supplying a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `cursor=0:-3:0`, which Cursor.from_string parses happily) to the optimized path gets a 500; the advertised 'negative offset pagination' feature is architecturally impossible over a Django queryset and can never work as designed.

[BUG] The set-to-zset migration reuses the identical Redis key names (`span-buf:s:{project_and_trace}:{span_id}`) while switching the encoding — this diff writes zsets via zadd/zscan/zcard into keys that the pre-deploy code creates and reads as sets via sadd/sscan. During a rolling deploy every cross-version access raises WRONGTYPE ResponseError — old sadd/sscan against zset keys and new zadd/zscan against set keys — crashing span buffering and flushing across the fleet for the deploy window, and keys written before the deploy keep breaking the new code until their TTL expires; the key namespace needed versioning (a new prefix) to coexist.

[BUG] The Lua script's conversion to sorted sets is incomplete: the script's own span-insertion (`sadd(set_key, payload)` guarded by `not is_root_span`, unchanged below this hunk) still writes a SET into set_key, which the same script's new `zcard(set_key)` / `zunionstore` calls then access as a ZSET. The first add-buffer call for a parent creates set_key as a SET via the unchanged sadd, and the second call's `span_count == 0 -> zcard(set_key)` raises WRONGTYPE inside the script — every trace with two or more spans under the same parent fails to buffer, breaking span ingestion on the Lua path while the Python-path tests updated in this diff stay green.

[BUG] process_batch reads `val['end_timestamp_precise']` as a required key (unlike the `.get()` used for parent_span_id/is_remote) with no fallback to `end_timestamp`, while the diff's own test fixtures show the field being newly added to messages and the `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` performs no runtime validation of the contract. Any ingest-spans message produced without the field — messages in flight during a rolling deploy or producers on an older schema revision — raises KeyError inside process_batch, crashing the consumer batch and poison-pilling the partition until the offset is skipped.

[ADVISORY] Eviction via zpopmin permanently discards the oldest spans (lowest end_timestamp_precise) with no metric or log, replacing the flusher's loud all-or-nothing skip (metrics.incr + logger.error on segment_span_count_exceeded, deleted in this diff) with silent partial data loss. Long-lived segments that keep receiving spans silently lose their earliest spans before flush, producing partial traces in Snuba with no signal operators can alert on — the data-loss model changes from loud all-or-nothing to silent partial, and the dropped spans are unrecoverable.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-resolution loop bound is cut from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the correctness boundary ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') is deleted rather than updated. Span parent chains deeper than ~1001 redirects now silently attach spans to an intermediate segment instead of the resolved root, misattributing span data for deep-recursion traces that the previous bound handled — a 10x tightening of a documented correctness limit with no stated rationale.

[ADVISORY] The 1000-span cap is enforced only inside add-buffer.lua, while the process consumer's writer (process_spans zadd) performs no eviction and this diff simultaneously deletes the flusher's max_segment_spans guard — the cap is not enforced across writers, and the hardcoded 1000 in Lua silently replaces whatever max_segment_spans was configured to. Segments buffered via the process_spans path grow past any count bound (only the byte-size guard remains at flush), and operators who tuned max_segment_spans get a different, unconfigurable effective cap applied to only one of the two writers with no indication anything changed.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result line-for-line except for the negative-offset branch, while the diff's only edit to BasePaginator.get_result itself (the max(0, offset) clamp at lines 179-184) is a no-op for every legitimate cursor (offsets are always >= 0 from build_cursor) and is justified by a comment misstating Django slicing semantics. Every future fix to BasePaginator.get_result must be hand-mirrored into the copy, which already diverges within this diff, and the false 'querysets handle boundary conditions' comment invites reproducing the negative-slice crash in other paginators — the class, the endpoint branch that uses it, and the base-class edit should be deleted rather than maintained as a parallel paginator.

[ADVISORY] The diff's test changes only thread end_timestamp_precise through existing Python-path fixtures; no test in the diff exercises OptimizedCursorPaginator, the auditlogs optimized branch, or the Lua script's zset conversion and eviction at all. CI stays green while the Lua path (WRONGTYPE on the second buffered span) and the entire optimized-pagination path (NameError/TypeError/ValueError) are broken — a stand-in guard where the updated tests never execute the changed Lua or paginator code, so the defects ship undetected.

[BUG] The PR's declared objective is 'Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert', but the diff bundles an entirely unrelated admin-gated 'optimized pagination' feature for the audit-log endpoint (new OptimizedCursorPaginator class, a new endpoint branch, and cursor comments), silently changing the artifact's objective without any human acceptance of that second objective. Acceptance and review granted for a spans-buffer performance change are silently extended to a separate pagination feature that is itself broken (NameError on every audit-log request, TypeError/AssertionError 500s on its optimized path); the layered 'Performance optimization'/'Enable advanced pagination for admins' comments launder the smuggled scope as intentional. The pagination work must be split into its own reviewed PR or removed.

[BUG] The new gating line references `organization_context`, which is neither imported anywhere in the diff nor defined in the endpoint's `get` method, so the expression raises NameError. Because `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` executes unconditionally before the `use_optimized` check, every GET on the organization audit-log endpoint raises NameError and returns 500 for all users, taking the whole endpoint down, not just requests opting into the optimized path.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the key attribute, but the audit-log endpoint's key is `datetime` (a datetime object), so `math.floor(value)` raises TypeError ('datetime doesn't define __floor__'). Every optimized_pagination request that returns any rows crashes with a 500 while build_cursor computes the next/prev cursor — the feature fails on its very first page, not on an edge case; the class copied CursorPaginator's numeric-key handling into a role that previously required DateTimePaginator's datetime conversion.

[BUG] The 'advanced' branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` with `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), which Django forbids — QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.') — so the adjacent comment claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually false. Any authorized request carrying a cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses the client-supplied offset with no lower bound, and cursors.py in this diff even advertises negative offsets) returns a 500 instead of results; the advertised 'advanced feature' is unreachable without crashing.

[BUG] The redirect-resolution loop limit is cut from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the correctness tradeoff ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') is deleted, silently weakening a documented accepted constraint by 10x with no connection to the stated eviction objective. Spans in traces with parent chains deeper than 1000 now stop resolving mid-chain and are attached to an intermediate segment's set instead of the root segment, splitting traces — a failure mode the removed comment explicitly documented as tolerated only up to depth 10k; this objective change was never accepted.

[ADVISORY] The buffer's value type changes from set to zset in place under identical key names (`span-buf:s:{...}`), so keys written by the old code are SETs while the new code issues zcard/zunionstore/zscan/zadd against them, and old workers still running scard/sunionstore/sscan fail symmetrically on zsets written by new workers. During a rolling deploy and until all pre-deploy keys hit TTL, every touch of pre-existing buffered spans raises WRONGTYPE: buffered spans become unreadable and are dropped, both old and new workers emit error storms, and the diff contains no migration or key-versioning to manage the transition.

[ADVISORY] The flusher's span-count guard (max_segment_spans skip with metric and error log) is removed on the assumption that the new Lua-side 1000 cap makes it redundant, but eviction exists only inside the Lua script while the Python insert path (process_spans zadd, lines 197-199) adds spans with no eviction. A batch that pushes a segment past 1000 spans before the next script invocation produces an oversized segment that now reaches the flusher with no guard — reintroducing exactly the failure mode (oversized segment ingestion) that the removed guard and its segment_span_count_exceeded metric existed to catch.

[ADVISORY] Eviction via zpopmin silently discards the oldest spans with no metric or log, replacing the previous observable all-or-nothing failure mode (metrics.incr + logger.error + skip whole segment) with unobservable partial data loss. Operators lose the only signal that spans are being dropped; incomplete segments are ingested with no trace of why, making the production data-loss rate unmeasurable and undiagnosable.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises the PR's headline behavior — the >1000-span eviction (zpopmin) path or the reduced 1000-iteration redirect limit; every test change only adds end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures. A regression in the new eviction logic (evicting the wrong end, evicting everything, or never evicting) or in the depth-limit change ships silently, since the only new behavior-bearing logic in the spans half of the PR has zero coverage.

[ADVISORY] process_batch indexes `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` unconditionally, so any span message lacking the field raises KeyError. If older producers (pre-upgrade relay versions during a rolling deploy) still emit spans without end_timestamp_precise, every affected batch raises KeyError and the consumer stalls/restarts on the partition instead of ingesting; a `.get()` fallback to `timestamp` would preserve the old tolerance.

[ADVISORY] The shared CursorPaginator.get_result — used by every paginated endpoint — is modified with a comment claiming to 'allow negative offsets' while the code does the opposite (`max(0, offset)` clamps them), and the change is unrelated to the PR's spans-buffer objective. Future maintainers will read the comment and assume negative-offset slicing is supported, building on a premise the code rejects; meanwhile a silent behavior change (crafted negative-offset non-prev cursors now return page 0 instead of erroring) ships on a shared hot path with no test or justification tied to this PR's intent.

[ADVISORY] cursors.py gains only a comment asserting that negative offsets are 'allowed' for 'advanced pagination scenarios', but no code in the diff enables them — every paginator path either clamps negative offsets to 0 or crashes on them. The comment documents a nonexistent capability, sending the next reader hunting for behavior that does not exist and presenting the unrelated paginator changes as a deliberate cursor-level feature during review.

[ADVISORY] The new pagination behavior is gated on a raw query parameter (`optimized_pagination == "true"`) with no feature flag or options entry. If the optimized path misbehaves in production it cannot be disabled without a code deploy, and any user who learns the parameter name can flip their own requests onto the untested code path (subject only to the admin gate).

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates CursorPaginator.get_result wholesale (subclassing BasePaginator and re-implementing get_item_key, value_from_cursor, and the entire get_result body) solely to add the broken negative-offset branch. Two hand-maintained copies of the pagination core will drift independently (the shared-paginator clamp change in this same diff was not carried over consistently); the deletion test passes cleanly — removing the class and the endpoint branch deletes ~95 lines and every crash site while leaving the endpoint on DateTimePaginator exactly as before.

[ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator class and the endpoint's optimized_pagination branch have no tests in the diff — not even a single happy-path request. All three crash modes in the new path (NameError on the gate line, TypeError on datetime keys in get_item_key, AssertionError on negative-offset slices) would have been caught by one endpoint test; without it the broken feature ships unverified.

[ADVISORY] zunionstore replaces sunionstore, and Redis zunionstore sums scores when the same member appears in both source sets, so a payload present in both merged sets acquires a summed (corrupted) end_timestamp score that set-union semantics never produced. Redelivered spans that land in two sets before a merge get inflated timestamps, skewing the eviction order so the wrong spans are evicted first; sunionstore was idempotent for members, zunionstore is not score-preserving.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch passes the user-controlled cursor offset (Cursor.from_string parses the cursor's offset component with plain int() and accepts negatives) straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], and Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ unconditionally raises ('Negative indexing is not supported') for any negative slice start, so the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false and this branch can never execute successfully. adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua`, merges previously done via `sunionstore` are now done via `zunionstore` (e.g. `span_count = redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` and similarly for `parent_key`) without specifying `WEIGHTS`/`AGGREGATE`. Redis `ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`, so if the same `span.payload` member exists in both source zsets, its score (now `end_timestamp_precise` per `buffer.py` `zadd`) will be summed, inflating/corrupting the timestamp score. Since the diff also introduces eviction based on score order (`zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`), this can change which spans are evicted first, producing incorrect behavior compared to the previous idempotent set union semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The negative-offset branch passes the user-controlled cursor offset (Cursor.from_string parses the cursor's offset component with plain int() and accepts negatives) straight into queryset[start_offset:stop], and Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ unconditionally raises ('Negative indexing is not supported') for any negative slice start, so the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false and this branch can never execute successfully. Any superuser or global-access member who requests the audit-logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a negative-offset cursor (e.g. cursor=1700000000.0:-5:0) gets an unhandled AssertionError/ValueError and an HTTP 500 instead of a page; the advertised reverse-pagination feature returns no data, and the input-validation assumption the design relies on does not exist.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an explicit “negative offset” code path in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`: when `enable_advanced_features` and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (with `stop` derived from that negative start). The cursor offset is not validated in `Cursor.__init__` (it just does `self.offset = int(offset)`), so a negative value can reach this slice. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indexes, so this branch contradicts the inline comment (“Django ORM properly handles negative slicing”) and would raise at runtime, yielding a 500 for any request that reaches it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The clamp was applied to only one branch: the is_prev path still forwards a raw negative cursor offset into queryset[start_offset:stop], which Django rejects with 'Negative indexing is not supported', while the new comment directly above the changed lines asserts negative offsets are 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions'. Any authenticated user on any CursorPaginator endpoint can still trigger an unhandled 500 with a negative-offset prev cursor (a pre-existing crash this diff touched but left unfixed), and maintainers extending prev-cursor pagination will build on the false safety invariant written on the exact lines they are editing.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the new logic clamps negative offsets only when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). For `cursor.is_prev` it still forwards the raw `offset` into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, so a negative `cursor.offset` will result in negative QuerySet slicing. The diff also adds comments asserting negative offsets are “safe”/handled by the queryset (in both `paginator.py` and `utils/cursors.py`), which contradicts Django’s behavior (negative QuerySet indexing/slicing is not supported) and can still lead to an unhandled exception/500 on the prev-cursor path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The gate for the new optimized code path uses request.user.is_superuser (the static Django flag rather than is_active_superuser(request), which validates superuser elevation and expiry) or organization_context.member.has_global_access (a raw membership-role flag that ignores SSO validity and the computed scopes on request.access), bypassing the platform's authorization primitives. No data is exposed on this endpoint today because OrganizationAuditPermission already gates the handler before this line runs, but this is the only check guarding the new code path and the pattern invites copy-paste into handlers where it would be the sole gate, letting SSO-invalid or un-elevated sessions select non-standard behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new optimized code path is enabled via `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` and a user-controlled query param `optimized_pagination` (see added block before `self.paginate`). The diff shows this gate does not use any request-scoped authorization primitive (e.g., `request.access` / computed scopes) and relies on raw flags. While the endpoint is still guarded earlier by `OrganizationAuditPermission` (as the finding notes), the concern about introducing a pattern that bypasses stronger auth/elevation/SSO-aware checks for selecting privileged behavior is grounded in the change itself. The diff alone doesn’t prove an actual exploit or data exposure here, but it is a concrete review issue created by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] process_batch reads end_timestamp_precise with a bare val['end_timestamp_precise'] subscript and the cast(SpanEvent, ...) performs no validation, so any ingest-spans message produced without the field — e.g. by pre-deploy producers during a rolling deploy — raises KeyError. The unhandled exception fails the arroyo batch before offsets are committed, so the consumer restarts and reprocesses the same poison message indefinitely, stalling that partition of the spans pipeline (and every span behind it) until manual intervention.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py`, `process_batch` now does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))` and then unconditionally reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` when constructing `Span`. The `cast(...)` adds no runtime validation, and there is no `.get(...)`/default/try-except. Therefore, any message lacking `end_timestamp_precise` will raise a `KeyError` at runtime, failing processing for that batch/message. The diff also makes `Span.end_timestamp_precise` a required field (no default) in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`, reinforcing that this will crash rather than degrade gracefully.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new OptimizedCursorPaginator (~95 lines of offset arithmetic, prev-cursor trimming, and cursor construction) has no test anywhere in this diff — the test changes only add end_timestamp_precise fixtures to span-buffer/consumer tests — and its first real invocation already crashes (math.ceil on the datetime key produced by order_by='-datetime' raises TypeError, and the negative-offset branch raises on Django slicing). Nothing in CI exercises the admin-selectable path, so it ships broken and stays broken; future changes to the trim logic (len(results) == offset + limit + extra, which is already wrong for negative offsets) or to key handling would silently return wrong pages with no regression signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and immediately wires it into `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get()` when `optimized_pagination=true` for privileged users, using `order_by="-datetime"`. However `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` does `math.floor/ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`, which for audit logs is very likely a `datetime` field (`datetime`), not a number—this would raise a `TypeError` at runtime. Additionally, the new negative-offset slicing path (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset` may be negative) is risky because Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices, making this path likely to crash as well. No tests in this diff exercise this new paginator or the admin-selectable optimized path, so these failures would not be caught by CI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test executes the eviction branch added in this diff: the test files that drive add-buffer.lua (tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py, tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py) insert at most 6 spans per set, so `span_count > 1000` is never reached and the `zpopmin` trim — the feature named in the PR title — runs zero times across the entire suite. A defect in the eviction arithmetic (off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, trimming the wrong key, or evicting newest instead of oldest spans) permanently drops spans that would otherwise be flushed, and every test still passes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new eviction/trim branch in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`: after merging via `zunionstore`, it computes `span_count` and, if `span_count > 1000`, executes `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`. The updated/added tests shown in the diff (e.g., `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py`, `test_flusher.py`) only construct very small span sets (a handful of spans per segment), and nothing in these changes drives `span_count` above 1000, so this new eviction path is not exercised by the tests in this diff. That’s a concrete coverage gap for nontrivial new behavior, not a directly verifiable defect in the arithmetic itself. The claim that it runs zero times across the *entire* suite can’t be proven from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Every fixture touched in this diff uses a single uniform score (1700000000.0 in test_buffer.py and test_consumer.py, `now` in test_flusher.py) and no assertion anywhere inspects a zset score, so the score semantics introduced by the sadd→zadd migration are completely unverified even on paths the tests do execute. Score-corrupting behavior passes the whole suite: ZUNIONSTORE's default SUM aggregation (add-buffer.lua:47 and :53) adds two ~1.7e9 timestamps whenever a payload exists in both merged sets — e.g. self-parent spans where span_key == set_key doubles every score — and zpopmin then evicts by corrupted order, but flushed output contains only members, so no current assertion can detect it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes span buffering from SETs to ZSETs with scores based on `end_timestamp_precise` (Python `zadd`), and the Lua merge path uses `ZUNIONSTORE set_key 2 set_key span_key` / `... parent_key` without an `AGGREGATE` option. In Redis, `ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`, so if a member/payload exists in both inputs its score will be summed (corrupting a timestamp-like score). Since the script then enforces a size cap via `ZPOPMIN` based on score ordering, summed scores can change which spans get evicted. The tests added in the diff only provide uniform scores and never assert on score/ordering/eviction behavior, so this bug would not be detected by the current suite.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] This diff deletes the max_segment_spans overflow guard in _load_segment_data (the metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded") + error-log + skip-segment branch) and the only buffer test file touched (tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py) contains no change exercising the span-count limit, so neither the removal of the skip behavior nor the new load-everything behavior is verified. Segments exceeding the span-count limit are now loaded in full instead of skipped, changing flush-time memory behavior and silently removing the guard metric; a regression that reintroduces a cap or exhausts memory on huge segments is invisible to the suite.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the span-count overflow guard in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data`: the block that checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`, emitted `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")`, logged, and skipped the segment is deleted, and the new code simply does `payloads[key].extend(span for span, _ in zscan_values)` with no equivalent cap/skip/metric. While the Lua changes add a zset trimming step (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(...) end`), that is a different location/threshold than `self.max_segment_spans` and does not, from this diff alone, prove the Python-side guard is now redundant. The test updates in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` only add `end_timestamp_precise` fields and do not add coverage for oversized segments or the removed metric/skip behavior, so this behavioral change is not verified by the suite.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py only feeds payloads that contain end_timestamp_precise, so the required key access val["end_timestamp_precise"] is never exercised against a payload lacking the field. During a rolling deploy where old producers still emit the previous ingest_spans_v1 payload (or when replaying old topic data), process_batch raises KeyError on every such message; the producer/consumer coupling is untested, so a schema mismatch ships undetected.

adjudication.rationale: In `process_batch` the diff changes to a required dict access `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` (src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py), so any message lacking that key will raise `KeyError`. The updated tests in `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py` only ever include `end_timestamp_precise`, so they don’t exercise or document behavior for older/malformed payloads (no fallback like `val.get(...)` or defaulting). Whether old Kafka messages/producers exist is not verifiable from this diff, but the introduced hard requirement + lack of coverage/compat handling is a concrete review concern grounded in the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-follow loop limit drops from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the mis-join consequence is deleted, while the deepest test in tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py (test_deep) chains only 5 spans — nothing approaches or crosses the new boundary. Traces with parent chains deeper than 1000 (or redirect cycles) now silently join into wrong segment sets with no test detecting the boundary change, and any future edit to this constant has no coverage to regress against.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` reduces the redirect-follow loop from `for i = 0, 10000 do` (with an explicit comment warning about deep chains) to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and removes that warning. There is no new handling for the case where the loop exhausts without hitting the `break`, so deeper redirect chains would now stop earlier and proceed with whatever `set_span_id` value was last seen, potentially changing join behavior for chains >1000 compared to before. The existing tests shown (`tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py::test_deep`) only build very shallow chains (5 spans), so there is no coverage guarding this boundary change or documenting intent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] add-buffer.lua replaces scard/sunionstore with zcard/zunionstore on the same span-buf:s:* key namespace, so during a rolling deploy the script aborts with WRONGTYPE the moment it touches a key that pre-deploy workers created as a SET. Redis halts the script at the first zcard against a legacy SET key (commands already executed, e.g. the main_redirect_key hset at line 40, are not rolled back on a runtime script error), so spans routed through legacy keys fail to buffer and the ingestion path errors until every legacy key expires via TTL; there is no key-namespace bump, dual-format handling, or conversion step anywhere in the diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type used for the `span-buf:s:{...}:*` keys from SETs to ZSETs: `buffer.py` switches `sadd`→`zadd` and `sscan`→`zscan`, and `add-buffer.lua` switches `scard/sunionstore`→`zcard/zunionstore` on the same key namespace (`span-buf:s:{%s}:%s`). There is no namespace bump, migration, or dual-read/write logic in the diff. During a rolling deploy, pre-deploy workers can leave existing `span-buf:s:*` keys as SETs, and the updated Lua script will then hit `zcard`/`zunionstore` on those legacy SET keys, which in Redis triggers `WRONGTYPE` and aborts the script. The diff contains no safeguards to avoid this mixed-type failure mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] _load_segment_data now issues zscan against span-buf:s:* keys that the review-base code populated as SETs, and Redis raises WRONGTYPE for any key still holding set-encoded data. p.execute() raises on the first WRONGTYPE in the batch, so the entire flush batch fails: legacy-format segments are never flushed and their buffered spans are silently lost when the key's expire TTL lapses, and even new ZSET keys sharing the same batch are blocked from flushing until the legacy keys drain — the existing SET-format data has no migration or dual-format read path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes span buffer storage for `span-buf:s:{...}:*` from Redis SETs to ZSETs: `process_spans` switches `p.sadd(...)` to `p.zadd(...)`, and `_load_segment_data` switches `p.sscan(...)` to `p.zscan(...)`. There is no dual-read path, type check, or migration for pre-existing keys created by the old code. If any legacy keys still exist as SETs when the new code runs, `zscan` on a SET will raise Redis `WRONGTYPE`, and because it’s executed inside a pipeline (`p.execute()`), a single wrong-typed key would fail the batch. This matches the finding’s claim that legacy-format segments would fail to flush until they expire.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_spans writes with p.zadd into the same keys old workers populate via sadd, so any zadd that lands on a key still typed as SET raises WRONGTYPE and fails the whole pipeline batch. During the mixed-version deploy window new workers crash buffering spans onto legacy keys (and old workers' sadd/sunionstore symmetrically fail on ZSETs new workers created), stalling span processing until legacy keys expire; the format change is applied in place with no expand phase, so old and new code cannot coexist on the shared keyspace.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type used for the same key pattern `span-buf:s:{...}:{...}` from SET to ZSET: `process_spans` switches `p.sadd(...)` to `p.zadd(...)` (buffer.py), reads switch from `sscan` to `zscan`, and the Lua script switches `scard/sunionstore` to `zcard/zunionstore` and trims via `zpopmin`. There is no key versioning/rename, no dual-write/dual-read, and no migration/expand phase shown. If any old code still uses `SADD/SSCAN/SUNIONSTORE` against keys that new code has created as ZSETs (or vice versa), Redis will raise `WRONGTYPE` and pipeline execution would fail for that batch. This mixed-version incompatibility is directly implied by the in-place type change on the same keys.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new zpopmin eviction permanently deletes the lowest-score (oldest) spans from a segment's buffer set with no metric, log, or flush, and can evict a span whose children were already merged into the same set. Accepted spans are silently discarded without ever reaching storage — the removed flush-time guard at least emitted segment_span_count_exceeded and logged an error before skipping, while this path drops data with zero observability — and evicting a span whose children remain in the set (possible whenever a child's end_timestamp_precise exceeds its parent's) orphans those children, producing incomplete traces.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a hard cap in `add-buffer.lua` that evicts spans via `zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`, permanently deleting the lowest-score entries (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) with no metric/log/flush path (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", ...) end`). At the same time, the previous flush-time protection/observability for oversized segments is removed in `_load_segment_data` (deleted `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric + error log + skip logic). This makes span loss silent and directly introduced by the change. Because ordering is by `end_timestamp_precise` (child spans can legitimately have later end timestamps than parents), evicting the “oldest” by end time can remove a parent while keeping children in the same zset, plausibly producing orphaned/incomplete traces.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch reads end_timestamp_precise with direct subscript val["end_timestamp_precise"] instead of a defaulted .get() like the adjacent parent_span_id/is_remote fields, so any ingest_spans message produced without that field raises KeyError inside process_batch. Old-format messages still inside Kafka retention when the new consumer deploys (or lagging producers during the rolling deploy) crash the processing strategy; on restart arroyo resumes from the same offset and crashes again, crash-looping the consumer and stalling that partition's span processing until the poison message is manually skipped.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py` `process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` while adjacent fields use `.get(...)` (e.g. `parent_span_id=val.get("parent_span_id")`). If an ingested span payload lacks `end_timestamp_precise`, this will raise `KeyError` and fail the batch processing. The diff also makes `Span.end_timestamp_precise` a required `NamedTuple` field (no default), reinforcing that missing data will crash rather than degrade gracefully.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-resolution loop bound is cut from 10000 to 1000, so redirect chains deeper than 1000 that legacy code could resolve now exhaust the loop and spans attach to an intermediate segment instead of the root. Existing chains persisted in main_redirect_key (still within TTL at deploy time) deeper than the new bound are mis-resolved and spans are misparented during trace assembly; the comment documenting the 10k tradeoff was deleted rather than updated to the tighter limit, so the next maintainer loses the record of this failure mode.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does reduce the redirect-resolution loop in `add-buffer.lua` from `for i = 0, 10000 do` (with an explicit comment about the 10k-depth tradeoff) to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and removes that explanatory comment. This is a behavior change: chains deeper than 1000 will no longer be fully followed and `set_span_id` may remain at an intermediate redirect target. However, the claim that such >1000-deep chains exist (including persisted ones within TTL at deploy time) is not verifiable from the diff alone, so it’s better treated as an edge-case/compatibility concern plus lost documentation rather than a confirmed defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The eviction path (the span_count==0 zcard fallback and the zpopmin truncation) ships with no test coverage — every test change in this diff only adds end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures, and no test drives a set past 1000 members. A regression in the count math or the fallback (e.g. truncating after a merge that mis-counts cardinality) would silently truncate live segment buffers in production with no failing test to catch it first, compounding the already-unobservable nature of the eviction.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new nontrivial eviction/truncation logic in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`: it tracks `span_count`, falls back to `zcard` when merges didn’t occur (`if span_count == 0 then span_count = redis.call("zcard", set_key) end`), and then truncates to 1000 with `zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`. The test changes shown only update fixtures to include the new `end_timestamp_precise` field and do not add any scenario that drives a buffer past 1000 members or exercises the merge+fallback counting behavior, so this new eviction path is indeed untested in this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Every request to the audit-logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true crashes with a 500: OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator, which provides none of the cursor machinery its body calls (build_queryset, count_hits, key, desc, _is_asc, max_limit are implemented on CursorPaginator/Paginator), and the endpoint passes order_by='-datetime' — a Paginator-style kwarg that neither sets key/desc nor is accepted by BasePaginator.__init__ — so construction or first use raises TypeError/AttributeError/NotImplementedError. Any superuser or global-access member sending optimized_pagination=true to the audit-logs endpoint gets a raw 500; the new pagination feature is dead on arrival, and even if the wiring were fixed, get_item_key would still raise TypeError because math.floor/math.ceil are applied to the raw datetime 'datetime' field instead of converting to epoch seconds like DateTimePaginator does.

adjudication.rationale: The diff wires `organization_auditlogs.get()` to use `OptimizedCursorPaginator` when `optimized_pagination=true` for privileged users, passing `order_by='-datetime'` and `enable_advanced_features=True`. However, the newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator` subclasses `BasePaginator` yet its implementation calls cursor-paginator-specific machinery/attributes (`build_queryset`, `count_hits`, `max_limit`, `desc`, `key`, `_is_asc`, `post_query_filter`, `on_results`) that are not shown as part of `BasePaginator` in this diff. Even if construction succeeds, `get_item_key()` does `math.floor/math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`, and with `order_by='-datetime'` on audit log rows that value will be a `datetime`, which is not compatible with `floor/ceil` (unlike `DateTimePaginator` which typically converts datetimes to a numeric cursor). This makes the new optimized path very likely to raise at runtime (TypeError/AttributeError), yielding 500s when the flag is used.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start (list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) with start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which raises Django's AssertionError 'Negative indexing is not supported.' — the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. Once the paginator is reachable, the feature's advertised capability (negative offsets, e.g. a client-supplied cursor like 0:-1:0, which Cursor.from_string accepts without validation) 500s on its own happy path, and the else-branch still passes negative offsets through for is_prev cursors, crashing the same way.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py`, the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing/slicing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.`. Additionally, even outside that branch, both the updated existing paginator logic and the optimized paginator use `start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, which will pass a negative `offset` through unchanged whenever `cursor.is_prev` is true, causing the same negative-slice failure path. The diff also adds commentary in `Cursor.__init__` suggesting negative offsets are intended and does not add validation/clamping to prevent negatives.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Eviction via zpopmin silently discards the oldest spans with no metric or log, and the diff simultaneously deletes the flusher-side overflow signal (the segment_span_count_exceeded metric plus error log in _load_segment_data), so buffer overflow went from logged-and-counted to completely invisible. Operators debugging missing spans from high-volume traces (>1000 spans per segment) get zero signal that eviction is occurring or how much data is being dropped; the byte-size overflow metric remains but the count-based one is gone, so eviction storms are undetectable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce silent span dropping without any explicit metric/log. In `add-buffer.lua`, after computing `span_count`, it enforces a hard cap with `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` when `span_count > 1000`, but does not emit any metric/log about how many spans were evicted. At the same time, in `spans/buffer.py` `_load_segment_data`, the previous span-count overflow signal was removed: the block that checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans:` and emitted `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` plus `logger.error(...)` was deleted, and the code now just extends payloads from `zscan` values. This makes span-count-based overflow/eviction effectively invisible to operators. However, the eviction itself appears intentional (a new cap), so the issue is primarily missing observability rather than a directly verifiable correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The shared Paginator's behavior changes for every endpoint that uses the default paginator: a forward cursor with a negative offset now silently clamps to offset 0 and returns the first page instead of erroring, while is_prev cursors with negative offsets still raise Django's negative-slicing AssertionError — an unrelated shared-component behavior change smuggled into the spans PR and only half-applied. Clients with corrupted or hand-crafted forward cursors silently receive page 1 (masking their bug) on every Paginator-based endpoint, while the identical malformed cursor sent as a prev cursor still 500s — inconsistent, undocumented, and justified by a comment ('the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') that describes behavior the queryset does not have.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes shared pagination behavior in `src/sentry/api/paginator.py:get_result` from `queryset[offset:stop]` to clamping `start_offset = max(0, offset)` for non-`cursor.is_prev` cursors, while still using `offset` directly for `cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). This means a negative `cursor.offset` on forward pagination is silently coerced to 0 (returning the first page) whereas a negative offset on a `prev` cursor can still hit Django's unsupported negative slicing behavior. This is a real, diff-grounded inconsistency/semantics change in a shared component, but it primarily affects malformed/hand-crafted cursors rather than valid inputs, so it’s better classified as a non-bug but important review concern (scope/behavior change and inconsistent error handling).
